title: Hold every hour
hook: take hold of each hour, Seneca begins, and you'll depend less on tomorrow

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lucilius, in Sicily, to whom Seneca wrote. Your line was dear friend. Did your short letter go out? Day four hundred thirty-two.

Open the screen-time report on your phone and it will tell you, to the minute, where your week went. Most people look once, wince, and never open it again. Seneca didn't have the report. He had something like it in his own head, and in the very first letter to Lucilius he opens it and makes himself look. The first lesson of a hundred twenty-four isn't about God or virtue. It's about time, and where ours keeps going. Today: hold every hour.

First, the opening command. Letter one begins, in Latin, vindica te tibi: claim yourself for yourself. The word vindica is a legal word, used for claiming property, or claiming a person's freedom in court. Seneca is telling Lucilius to take himself back, the way you'd take back something that had been taken from you. Second, the three thieves. Some of our time, Seneca says, is torn away from us, some is quietly stolen, and some just slips through our fingers. And the most shameful loss is the one that comes from carelessness. He adds that most of life passes doing the wrong thing, much of it doing nothing, and all of it doing something other than what we meant to. Third, the grasp. Then the line that gives this day its name. In Gummere's translation: hold every hour in your grasp. Take hold of today's work, Seneca says, and you'll depend less on tomorrow's. Year one gave us the sentence that follows soon after: nothing is ours except time. Fourth, the honesty. Seneca doesn't pretend he's mastered it. He tells Lucilius he keeps accounts of his own time, the way someone free-handed but careful keeps a household budget. He can't boast that he wastes nothing, he says, but he can tell you what he's wasting, and why. He's not preaching from a mountaintop. He's a man in his sixties, honest about his losses, and starting today. That's what holding an hour looks like: not a perfect schedule, just taking the next one in your hand.
screen: `VINDICA TE TIBI: CLAIM YOURSELF.` · `TORN AWAY, STOLEN, SLIPPED AWAY.` · `HOLD EVERY HOUR IN YOUR GRASP.` · `SENECA KEEPS HIS OWN ACCOUNTS.` · then, large: `HOLD THIS HOUR.`

segments.voice: Look at the clock. Note the time. Now think about the next hour of your day, the real one, not the ideal one. What is it actually going to hold? Pick one thing that hour is for: the report, the walk, the meal with your family, sleep. Picture yourself doing it fully. Then picture the thief that usually shows up, the scroll, the side errand, the drift. Decide now what you'll do when it knocks. Breathe, and hold the hour in your hand before it starts. The bell holds the time.
Three thieves, Seneca says, take your time: some torn away, some stolen quietly, some just slipping through carelessness. Today's word.
Your line: hold this hour. Use the next hour fully for the one thing you chose. When it ends, ask where it went, the way Seneca kept his accounts. Day four hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Seneca often keep a simple account of their time, noticing where the day went in the evening, and try to give each hour a purpose before it begins.

myth: Seneca's first letter is mainly about the gods
it's about time: claiming it back and holding each hour. death comes up only as part of that.
vindica is a legal word for claiming property or freedom
Seneca tells Lucilius to claim himself back, as if in court.
Seneca claims he never wastes time
he admits losses; he only says he can account for where it went.

fork.setup: you're Lucilius. your old friend writes that you're letting your time be stolen. what's the first thing he tells you to do?
options: claim yourself back and hold every hour.
fork.reveal: letter one opens with vindica te tibi, claim yourself for yourself, and then: hold every hour in your grasp.

original.note: Latin: claim yourself for yourself, the first words of advice in Seneca's first letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: time management, ancient edition.
what it means: Seneca tells Lucilius to claim himself back from the thieves of time and hold each hour, so he depends less on tomorrow.
what a scholar hears: vindicare is a legal verb for claiming property or asserting someone's freedom; Seneca uses law-court language for the self.

sources.quoted: hold every hour in your grasp.

notes: Gummere 1917, Letter 1.2: 'hold every hour in your grasp.' Checked against the Wikisource Gummere text (lowercase, mid-sentence after 'do as you write me that you are doing:'); quotation now matches. Confirm.
Hook originally said letter one is not about death; Letter 1.2 does discuss dying daily, so the hook and myth were adjusted to say it is about time, with death as part of that.

Letter 1.1: 'Ita fac, mi Lucili: vindica te tibi'; the three losses (eripiuntur, subducuntur, effluunt) and the most shameful loss through carelessness; 1.4: Seneca keeps account of his expenses of time. Paraphrased; confirm.
'Nothing is ours except time' (Letter 1.3) was used in year one (Gummere quotation in earlier scripts).
'In his sixties' assumes a birth c. 4 BCE and letters c. 63–65 CE; confirm.
Vindicare as a legal verb (vindicatio; vindicta in manumission): standard; confirm.
